questions.solution: beled explanation image below to review your anatomy. The retinal ganglion cell axons from the temporal half of the right eye retina (serving the left visual hemifield) and the retinal ganglion cell axons from the nasal half of the left eye retina (serving the left visual hemifield) project via the right optic tract to the right LGN. The corresponding afferent inputs to the pupillary light reflex exit the optic tract (destined for the pretectal nucleus) via the brachium of the superior colliculus BEFORE reaching the LGN. For this reason, a lesion involving only the right LGN will NOT cause a left afferent pupillary defect (APD) while a right optic tract lesion anterior to the brachium of the superior colliculus will cause a left APD. A lesion destroying the entire LGN would cause a complete contralateral homonymous hemianopia. The reality, however, is that clinically LGN lesions are exceptionally rare and when they do occur they typically involve only a portion of the LGN leading to a “sectoranopia” which is essentially a wedge shaped homonymous defect. A left afferent pupillary defect, also known as a Marcus Gunn pupil, results from damage to the optic nerve or severe retinal disease in one eye. The lesion described in the question is not related to pupillary function or the optic nerve. Option B- Hearing loss in the right ear: The lesion described in the question is not associated with the auditory system or the structures responsible for hearing. Therefore, hearing loss in the right ear is not a sequela of the lesion. Option D- A complete right homonymous hemianopia: This option is incorrect. The lesion's location, just medial to the tip of the green arrow, is on the left side of the brain. A right homonymous hemianopia would result from a lesion on the right side of the brain affecting the left optic tract or the right visual cortex. Option E-Bilateral hearing loss: As mentioned earlier, the lesion's location is not related to the auditory system or structures involved in hearing. questions.solution: Correct Option B- A homonymous right superior quadrantanopia: The left optic radiations serving vision in the right hemifield (in both eyes) originate in the left lateral geniculate nucleus and project to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe. Fibers serving the superior right quadrant of vision (in both eyes) project through the left temporal lobe in a structure known as the loop of Meyer which passes anteriorly as far as approximately 2.5 cm from the tip of the temporal lobe. Fibers serving the inferior right quadrant of vision (in both eyes) project through the parietal lobe to the primary visual cortex. Lesions of the optic tracts classically cause incongruous (asymmetric between the two eyes) field defects because the visual pathway fibers serving corresponding points in space are not closely approximated. In other words, the more posterior the lesion of the retrochiasmal visual pathways, the more organized the visual pathways fibers are and the more congruous (or symmetric) the visual field defects tend to be. Indeed, occipital lobe lesions tend to cause very congruous homonymous field defects. Lesions of the optic tract anterior to the brachium of the superior colliculus are expected to cause an incongruous contralateral homonymous hemianopic field defect AND a contralateral afferent pupillary defect. The afferent input to the pupillary light reflex, however, separates from the visual pathways just anterior to the lateral geniculate nucleus. Therefore, retrogeniculate optic pathway lesions AND pure lateral geniculate nucleus lesions (not involving the optic tract) do not affect pupillary function. Incorrect Options: Option A- A homonymous right inferior quadrantanopia: This option is incorrect because the lesion described in the question involves the anterior portion of the left temporal lobe. Lesions in this area would affect the fibers that carry visual information from the superior right quadrant of the visual field in both eyes. As a result, a homonymous right superior quadrantanopia would be expected, not an inferior quadrantanopia. Option C- A monocular right inferior quadrantanopia in the right eye only: Monocular field defects are not caused by lesions in the brain but rather by abnormalities in the eye itself or along the optic nerve. The lesion described in the question is located in the anterior portion of the left temporal lobe, which is a cerebral region. Therefore, monocular field defects would not be expected. questions.stem: A mass lesion simulated by the green oval on this coronal MRI image would be expected to result in what type of visual field defect?
questions.stemHtml: A mass lesion simulated by the green oval on this coronal MRI image would be expected to result in what type of visual field defect?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- A heteronymous bitemporal hemianopia: The coronal T1 post contrast MRI slice shown passes through the sellar region and the green lesion arising from the sella turcica can be seen involving the central portion of the optic chiasm sitting just superiorly. This lesion is therefore meant to simulate a sellar mass compressing the optic chiasm which classically results in a bitemporal hemianopic visual field defect. Retinal ganglion cell (RGC) axons passing through each optic nerve organize into nasal retinal fibers and temporal retinal fibers as they pass posteriorly from the optic nerve towards the optic chiasm. At the optic chiasm the nasal RGC axons (serving the temporal fields in both eyes) decussate while the temporal RGC axons do NOT decussate and pass onto the ipsilateral optic tract. For still unclear reasons, optic chiasm lesions clinically seem to preferentially affect the decussating RGC fibers such that chiasmal lesions classically result in a bitemporal pattern of visual field loss. A severe lesion of the optic chiasm obliterating all RGC fibers would, of course, cause bilateral complete blindness. In clinical practice evidence of a bitemporal hemianopic field defect is extremely helpful in localizing the pathology to the optic chiasm region. Incorrect Options: Option A- A homonymous left hemianopic defect: This option is incorrect because a left hemianopic defect would result from a lesion in the right optic tract or the left optic radiation. It would cause loss of vision in the left visual field in both eyes, not a bitemporal hemianopia. Option B- A homonymous right hemianopic defect: This option is also incorrect for the same reason as option A. A right hemianopic defect would occur with a lesion in the left optic tract or the right optic radiation, leading to loss of vision in the right visual field in both eyes. Option C- A heteronymous binasal hemianopia: This option is incorrect because a binasal hemianopia is a rare visual field defect that involves loss of vision in the inner (nasal) half of the visual field in both eyes. It is typically seen with lesions at the level of the optic chiasm's anterior portion, affecting the crossing nasal fibers. Option E- Bilateral central scotomas: This option is not related to the described lesion in the image. Bilateral central scotomas are characterized by a loss of central vision in both eyes, often seen in conditions affecting the macula, such as macular degeneration. It does not match the described lesion in the sellar region causing bitemporal hemianopia @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: Reduced median nerve CMAP amplitudes on routine NCSs would be likely in all of the following scenarios except?

options.label: A
options.text: A gunshot wound to the median nerve at the elbow, 5 weeks prior to presentation

options.label: B
options.text: Anterior horn cell disease presenting with four months of bilateral hand weakness

options.label: C
options.text: Critical illness (i.e., myosin loss) myopathy with quadriparesis

options.label: D
options.text: A severe C6 radiculopathy with eight weeks of right arm pain and weakness

questions.answerText: A severe C6 radiculopathy with eight weeks of right arm pain and weakness
questions.solution: Correct Option D- A severe C6 radiculopathy with eight weeks of right arm pain and weakness: Routine median motor NCSs record compound muscle action potentials from the abductor pollicis brevis (APB) muscle. The median nerve is composed of fibers that originate in the C6-T1 nerve roots. Motor fibers to the APB come from the C8-T1 nerve roots while the median motor fibers originating from the C6-7 roots innervate the pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis (FCR) muscles. Therefore, while a severe C6 radiculopathy would possibly result in pain and weak pronation/wrist flexion (as well as other potential motor deficits outside the proximal median distribution) with EMG evidence of denervation in the pronator teres and FCR muscles, it would have no effect on the APB and a normal median CMAP is therefore expected. All of the other listed options would be expected to result in small median CMAPs. Incorrect Options: Option A- A gunshot wound to the median nerve at the elbow, 5 weeks prior to presentation: In this scenario, the gunshot wound to the median nerve at the elbow could lead to axonal damage or disruption of the nerve fibers. This would likely result in reduced median compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs) in the affected nerve territory, which includes the muscles innervated by the median nerve below the injury site. Option B- Anterior horn cell disease presenting with four months of bilateral hand weakness: Anterior horn cell diseases affect the motor neurons in the spinal cord, leading to denervation of the muscles they innervate. In this case, the anterior horn cell disease is affecting the motor neurons that innervate the muscles of the hands, including those innervated by the median nerve. As a result, reduced median CMAPs would be expected due to denervation of the muscles in the hand. Option C- Critical illness (i.e., myosin loss) myopathy with quadriparesis: Critical illness myopathy is a neuromuscular disorder that can occur in critically ill patients. It results in muscle weakness and can lead to reduced CMAP amplitudes on nerve conduction studies (NCSs). If the myopathy affects the muscles innervated by the median nerve, it would result in reduced median CMAPs. Option E- Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome with bilateral hand weakness: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) is an autoimmune disorder that affects neuromuscular transmission. It is characterized by muscle weakness, especially in the proximal muscles. In LEMS, there is a decrease in the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, leading to reduced muscle activation. If the muscles innervated by the median nerve are affected, it would result in reduced median CMAPs. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit with severe systolic heart failure (ejection fraction of 15%). You are consulted for fluctuating hypersomnolence and periods of complete unresponsiveness. MRI shows acute infarction in the bilateral thalami. Which of these vascular variants is the most likely cause of these infarcts?

You are consulted for fluctuating hypersomnolence and periods of complete unresponsiveness. MRI shows acute infarction in the bilateral thalami. Which of these vascular variants is the most likely cause of these infarcts?

options.label: B
options.text: Fetal origin of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA)

options.label: D
options.text: Fenestration of the anterior communicating artery (ACOMM)

questions.solution: Correct Option C- Artery of Percheron: One important but rare variant of thalamic vascularization to recognize is the artery of Percheron where both paramedian arteries arise from a single trunk off one of the P1 segments. Clinically, this may lead to bithalamic infarcts from a single ischemic event. A persistent trigeminal artery is a retained anastomosis between the carotid artery and the basilar artery. A fetal PCA is a variant where the one or both PCAs feed from the anterior circulation, sometimes with a hypoplastic or absent P1 segment. A fenestrated ACOMM refers to a single ACOMM with two separate channels within the lumen. The azygous ACA variant occurs when there is a common A1 trunk originating from both ACAs with an associated absence of the anterior communicating artery. Incorrect Options: Option A- Persistent trigeminal artery: A persistent trigeminal artery is a rare anatomical variant where the trigeminal artery, which is an embryonic vessel, persists into adulthood. It connects the internal carotid artery with the basilar artery. However, it is not directly associated with the bilateral thalamic infarcts described in the clinical scenario. Option B- Fetal origin of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA): Fetal origin of the PCA is a variant where the PCA arises from the internal carotid artery instead of the basilar artery. Although this variant can have clinical significance, it is not the most likely cause of the bilateral thalamic infarcts described in the patient. Option D- Fenestration of the anterior communicating artery (ACOMM): A fenestrated ACOMM refers to a variation in the anterior cerebral circulation where the ACOMM, which connects the two anterior cerebral arteries (ACAs), has two separate channels within its lumen. While this is an interesting anatomical variant, it is not related to the infarcts in the bilateral thalami. Option E- Azygous anterior cerebral artery (ACA): The azygous ACA variant is a rare anatomical variation where there is a single A1 segment trunk that originates from both ACAs, with an associated absence of the anterior communicating artery. However, it is not the most likely cause of the bilateral thalamic infarcts described in the patient. @Neet_pg_bot

Nor is there a history of positional headache to suggest intracranial hypotension (treated with caffeine in some cases). questions.solution: Correct Option A - Cardiac conduction defects, pigmentary retinopathy, and disease onset before age 20 While there is considerable overlap in the features of mitochondrial cytopathies that present with CPEO, distinct differences in the hallmark features exist. All of these answer choices reflect the features of a syndrome that either always or sometimes present with CPEO. Kearns-Sayre syndrome is perhaps the best known syndrome associated with CPEO and is marked by the triad of CPEO, cardiac conduction defects, and pigmentary retinopathy. The disease onset (ptosis being the most visible) always occurs prior to the age 20. Interestingly the literature today supports the notion that CPEO, CPEO plus, and Kearns-Sayre Syndrome (KSS) all exist along a spectrum of disease. The earlier onset, more severe mitochondrial dysfunction manifests in a KSS phenotype while later onset disease may or may not be isolated to the extraocular muscles. questions.stem: What is the most common sleep disturbance in autistic spectrum disorders?
questions.stemHtml: What is the most common sleep disturbance in autistic spectrum disorders?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Insomnia: Insomnia (inadequate sleep) affects a majority of children with autistic spectrum disorder and can include difficulty falling asleep and/or difficulty sustaining sleep. Children with autistic disorders should be routinely screened for insomnia, and secondary causes, such as obstructive sleep apnea should be considered. Where appropriate, behavioral interventions and sleep hygiene should be offered, and should these approaches be ineffective, medications such as melatonin or clonidine may be considered. Incorrect Options: Option A- Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Obstructive sleep apnea involves repeated episodes of partial or complete upper airway obstruction during sleep, leading to disrupted breathing and frequent awakenings. While sleep apnea can occur in individuals with autism, it is not typically considered the most common sleep disturbance in this population. Option B- Central Sleep Apnea: Central sleep apnea is characterized by a lack of respiratory effort during sleep, leading to pauses in breathing. It is less common than obstructive sleep apnea and is not typically identified as the most common sleep disturbance in individuals with autism. Option D- Narcolepsy: Narcolepsy is a neurological disorder characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness, sudden episodes of muscle weakness (cataplexy), and sleep paralysis. While sleep problems can be present in individuals with autism, narcolepsy is not typically considered the most common sleep disturbance in this context. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B- Referring to an apple as a “pear”: This man is presenting with a language disorder typified by frequent phonemic paraphasias. Phonemic paraphasias are defined by words substituted by non-words that retain a notable percentage of the intended words morphemes. The alternate category of paraphasias are that of semantic paraphasias in which the word substituted for the intended word is an actual word and shares categorical similarities to the intended word (option b is therefore the correct answer in this case). Phonemic paraphasias are often seen in sensory/”Wernicke” aphasias, whereas both types of paraphasias are common in neurodegenerative disorders including the primary progressive aphasias (the agrammatic and behavioral variants representing forms of frontotemporal lobar degeneration whereas the logopenic variant is typically classified as a form of Alzheimer disease). The best examination technique used in assessing patients for this type of language abnormality is that of simple observation, as used in the example case above. If the patient doesn’t offer this option (i.e., paucity of speech) then formal means of assessment include the “cookie thief” picture used on the Boston Diagnostic Aphasia examination (now part of the cards used in generating the NIH stroke scale) or asking the patient to describe a picture of any other “scene” for that matter. Incorrect Options: Option A- Referring to an onion as an "um-yin": This is an example of a phonemic paraphasia . Phonemic paraphasias involve errors where individual sounds or phonemes within words are substituted, omitted, or rearranged. In this case, the sounds in "onion" are jumbled to produce "um-yin." Option C- Referring to a movie as a "moodie": This is also an example of a phonemic paraphasia , following the same pattern as the previous option. The "v" sound in "movie" is replaced with the "d" sound, resulting in "moodie." Option D- Referring to a pencil as a "pincer": This is a neologistic paraphasia . Neologistic paraphasias involve the creation of entirely new words that have no recognizable similarity to the intended word. In this case, "pincer" is a neologism unrelated to "pencil." @Neet_pg_bot
